{{Short description|Topic in mathematics}}
{{Information theory}}

In [[information theory]], the '''asymptotic equipartition property''' ('''AEP''') is a general property of the output samples of a [[stochastic process|stochastic source]]. It is fundamental to the concept of [[typical set]] used in theories of [[data compression]].

Roughly speaking, the theorem states that although there are many series of results that may be produced by a random process, the one actually produced is most probably from a loosely defined set of outcomes that all have approximately the same chance of being the one actually realized. (This is a consequence of the [[law of large numbers]] and [[ergodic theory]].) Although there are individual outcomes which have a higher probability than any outcome in this set, the vast number of outcomes in the set almost guarantees that the outcome will come from the set. One way of intuitively understanding the property is through [[Cramér's large deviation theorem]], which states that the probability of a large deviation from mean decays exponentially with the number of samples. Such results are studied in [[large deviations theory]]; intuitively, it is the large deviations that would violate equipartition, but these are unlikely.

In the field of [[Pseudorandom number generator|pseudorandom number generation]], a candidate generator of undetermined quality whose output sequence lies too far outside the typical set by some statistical criteria is rejected as insufficiently random. Thus, although the typical set is loosely defined, practical notions arise concerning ''sufficient'' typicality.

== Definition ==
Given a discrete-time stationary [[Ergodic process|ergodic]] stochastic process <math>X</math> on the [[probability space]] <math>(\Omega, B, p)</math>, the asymptotic equipartition property is an assertion that, [[almost sure|almost surely]],
<math display="block">-\frac{1}{n} \log p(X_1, X_2, \dots, X_n) \to H(X) \quad \text{ as } \quad n\to\infty</math>
where <math>H(X)</math> or simply <math>H</math> denotes the [[entropy rate]] of <math>X</math>, which must exist for all discrete-time [[stationary process]]es including the ergodic ones. The asymptotic equipartition property is proved for finite-valued (i.e. <math>|\Omega| < \infty</math>) stationary ergodic stochastic processes in the [[#Discrete-time finite-valued stationary ergodic sources|Shannon–McMillan–Breiman theorem]] using the ergodic theory and for any [[independent identically distributed random variables|i.i.d.]] sources directly using the law of large numbers in both the discrete-valued case (where <math>H</math> is simply the [[Entropy (information theory)|entropy]] of a symbol) and the continuous-valued case (where <math>H</math> is the [[differential entropy]] instead). The definition of the asymptotic equipartition property can also be extended for certain classes of continuous-time stochastic processes for which a typical set exists for long enough observation time. The convergence is proven [[almost sure]] in all cases.

== Discrete-time i.i.d. sources ==
Given <math>X</math> is an [[independent identically distributed random variables|i.i.d.]] source which may take values in the alphabet <math>\mathcal{X}</math>, its [[time series]] <math>X_1,\ldots,X_n</math> is i.i.d. with [[Entropy (information theory)|entropy]] <math>H(X)</math>. The weak [[law of large numbers]] gives the asymptotic equipartition property with [[convergence in probability]],
<math display="block">\lim_{n\to\infty}\Pr\left[\left|-\frac{1}{n} \log p(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n) - H(X)\right|> \varepsilon\right]=0 \qquad \forall \varepsilon > 0.</math>
since the entropy is equal to the expectation of {{sfnp|Cover|Thomas|1991|p=51}}
<math display="block">-\frac{1}{n} \log p(X_1, X_2, \ldots , X_n).</math>

The strong law of large numbers asserts the stronger almost sure convergence,
<math display="block">\Pr\left[\lim_{n\to\infty} - \frac{1}{n} \log p(X_1, X_2,\ldots, X_n) = H(X)\right]=1.</math>Convergence in the sense of L1 asserts an even stronger<math display="block">\mathbb{E} \left[\left|\lim_{n\to\infty} - \frac{1}{n} \log p(X_1, X_2,\ldots, X_n) - H(X)\right|\right]= 0</math>

== Discrete-time finite-valued stationary ergodic sources ==
Consider a finite-valued sample space <math>\Omega</math>, i.e. <math>|\Omega| < \infty</math>, for the discrete-time [[stationary ergodic process]] <math>X:=\{X_n\}</math> defined on the [[probability space]] <math>(\Omega, B, p)</math>. The '''Shannon–McMillan–Breiman theorem''', due to [[Claude Shannon]], [[Brockway McMillan]], and [[Leo Breiman]], states that we have convergence in the sense of L1.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Hawkins |first=Jane M. |author-link=Jane M. Hawkins |title=Ergodic dynamics: from basic theory to applications |date=2021 |publisher=Springer |isbn=978-3-030-59241-7 |series=Graduate texts in mathematics |location=Cham, Switzerland |pages=204}}</ref> [[Chung Kai-lai]] generalized this to the case where <math>X</math> may take value in a set of countable infinity, provided that the entropy rate is still finite.<ref name=":0">{{cite journal |last1=Algoet |first1=Paul H. |last2=Cover |first2=Thomas M. |author2-link=Thomas M. Cover |title=A Sandwich Proof of the Shannon–McMillan–Breiman Theorem |url=http://www-isl.stanford.edu/~cover/papers/paper83.pdf | archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20161206034835/http://www-isl.stanford.edu/~cover/papers/paper83.pdf | archive-date = 2016-12-06 | url-status = dead |journal=The Annals of Probability |volume=16 |issue=2 |pages=899–909 |year=1988|doi=10.1214/aop/1176991794| jstor=2243846 }}</ref>

{{math proof | title = Proof sketch<ref name=":0" />
|proof =
* Let ''x'' denote some measurable set <math>x = X(A)</math> for some <math>A \in B</math>
* Parameterize the joint probability by ''n'' and ''x'' as <math display="block">j(n,x):=p\left(x_0^{n-1} \right).</math>
* Parameterize the conditional probability by ''i'', ''k'' and ''x'' as <math display="block">c(i,k,x) := p \left (x_i\mid x_{i-k}^{i-1} \right).</math>
* Take the limit of the conditional probability as ''k'' → ∞ and denote it as <math display="block">c(i,x):=p \left(x_i\mid x_{-\infty}^{i-1} \right ).</math>
* Argue the two notions of entropy rate <math display="block">\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{1}{n} \mathrm{E}[-\log j(n,X)]\quad \text{and} \quad \lim_{n\to\infty} \mathrm{E}[-\log c(n,n,X)]</math> exist and are equal for any stationary process including the stationary ergodic process ''X''. Denote it as ''H''.
* Argue that both <math display="block">\begin{align}
c(i,k,X) &:= \left \{p \left(X_i\mid X_{i-k}^{i-1} \right ) \right \} \\
c(i,X) &:= \left \{p \left (X_i\mid X_{-\infty}^{i-1} \right ) \right \}
\end{align}</math> where ''i'' is the time index, are stationary ergodic processes, whose sample means converge [[almost surely]] to some values denoted by <math>H^k</math> and <math>H^{\infty}</math> respectively.
* Define the ''k''-th order Markov approximation to the probability <math>a(n,k,x)</math> as <math display="block">a(n,k,x) := p \left(X_0^{k-1} \right) \prod_{i=k}^{n-1}p \left (X_i\mid X_{i-k}^{i-1} \right )=j(k,x)\prod_{i=k}^{n-1} c(i,k,x)</math>
* Argue that <math>a(n,k,X(\Omega))</math> is finite from the finite-value assumption.
* Express <math>-\frac1n\log a(n,k,X)</math> in terms of the sample mean of <math>c(i,k,X)</math> and show that it converges almost surely to ''H<sup>k</sup>''
* Define the probability measure <math display="block">a(n,x):=p \left (x_0^{n-1}\mid x_{-\infty}^{-1} \right ).</math>
* Express <math>-\frac1n\log a(n,X)</math> in terms of the sample mean of <math>c(i,X)</math> and show that it converges almost surely to ''H<sup>∞</sup>''.
* Argue that <math>H^k\searrow H</math> as ''k'' → ∞ using the stationarity of the process.
* Argue that ''H'' = ''H''<sup>∞</sup> using the [[Lévy's martingale convergence theorem]] and the finite-value assumption.
* Show that <math display="block">\mathrm{E}\left[\frac{a(n,k,X)}{j(n,X)}\right]=a(n, k,X(\Omega))</math> which is finite as argued before.
* Show that <math display="block">\mathrm{E}\left[\frac{j(n,X)}{a(n,X)}\right]=1</math> by conditioning on the infinite past <math>X_{-\infty}^{-1}</math> and iterating the expectation.
* Show that <math display="block">\forall \alpha\in\mathbb{R} \ : \ \Pr\left[\frac{a(n,k,X)}{j(n,X)}\geq \alpha \right]\leq \frac{a(n, k,X(\Omega))}{\alpha}</math> using the [[Markov's inequality]] and the expectation derived previously.
* Similarly, show that <math display="block">\forall \alpha\in\mathbb{R} \ : \ \Pr\left[\frac{j(n,X)}{a(n,X)}\geq \alpha \right]\leq \frac{1}{\alpha},</math> which is equivalent to <math display="block">\forall \alpha\in\mathbb{R} \ : \ \Pr\left[\frac1n\log\frac{j(n,X)}{a(n,X)}\geq \frac{1}{n}\log\alpha \right]\leq \frac{1}{\alpha}.</math>
* Show that limsup of <math display="block">\frac1n \log \frac{a(n,k,X)}{j(n,X)} \quad \text{and} \quad \frac{1}{n} \log\frac{j(n,X)}{a(n,X)}</math> are non-positive almost surely by setting α = ''n''<sup>β</sup> for any β > 1 and applying the [[Borel–Cantelli lemma]].
* Show that liminf and limsup of <math display="block">-\frac{1}{n} \log j(n,X)</math> are lower and upper bounded almost surely by ''H<sup>∞</sup>'' and ''H<sup>k</sup>'' respectively by breaking up the logarithms in the previous result.
* Complete the proof by pointing out that the upper and lower bounds are shown previously to approach ''H'' as ''k'' → ∞.
}}

== Non-stationary discrete-time source producing independent symbols ==
The assumptions of stationarity/ergodicity/identical distribution of random variables is not essential for the asymptotic equipartition property to hold. Indeed, as is quite clear intuitively, the asymptotic equipartition property requires only some form of the law of large numbers to hold, which is fairly general. However, the expression needs to be suitably generalized, and the conditions need to be formulated precisely.

Consider a source that produces independent symbols, possibly with different output statistics at each instant, for which the statistics of the process are known completely, that is, the [[marginal distribution]] of the process seen at each time instant is known. The joint distribution is just the product of marginals. Then, under the condition (which can be relaxed) that <math>\mathrm{Var}[\log p(X_i)]<M</math> for all ''i'', for some ''M'' > 0, the following holds (AEP):
<math display="block">\lim_{n\to\infty}\Pr\left[\,\left|-\frac{1}{n} \log p(X_1, X_2, \ldots, X_n) - \overline{H}_n(X)\right|< \varepsilon\right]=1\qquad \forall \varepsilon > 0</math>
where 
<math display="block">\overline{H}_n(X)=\frac{1}{n}H(X_1,X_2,\ldots,X_n)</math>

{{math proof | proof =
The proof follows from a simple application of [[Markov's inequality]] (applied to second moment of <math>\log(p(X_i))</math>.
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\Pr \left[\left|-\frac{1}{n} \log p(X_1, X_2,\ldots, X_n) -\overline{H}(X)\right|> \varepsilon\right] &\leq \frac{1}{n^2 \varepsilon^2} \mathrm{Var} \left [\sum_{i=1}^n \log(p(X_i)) \right ]\\
&\leq \frac{M}{n \varepsilon^2} \to 0 \text{ as } n\to \infty
\end{align}</math>

It is obvious that the proof holds if any moment <math>\mathrm{E} \left [|\log p(X_i)|^r \right ]</math> is uniformly bounded for ''r'' > 1 (again by [[Markov's inequality]] applied to ''r''-th moment). [[Q.E.D.]]

Even this condition is not necessary, but given a non-stationary random process, it should not be difficult to test whether the asymptotic equipartition property holds using the above method.
}}

=== Applications ===
The asymptotic equipartition property for non-stationary discrete-time independent process leads us to (among other results) the [[source coding theorem]] for non-stationary source (with independent output symbols) and [[noisy-channel coding theorem]] for non-stationary memoryless channels.

== Measure-theoretic form ==
<math display="inline">T</math> is a measure-preserving map on the probability space <math display="inline">\Omega</math>.

If <math display="inline">P</math> is a finite or countable partition of <math display="inline">\Omega</math>, then its entropy is <math>H(P) := -\sum_{p \in P} \mu(p) \ln\mu(p)</math> with the convention that <math>0\ln 0 = 0</math>.

We only consider partitions with finite entropy: <math display="inline">H(P) < \infty</math>.

If <math display="inline">P</math> is a finite or countable partition of <math display="inline">\Omega</math>, then we construct a sequence of partitions by iterating the map:<math display="block">
      P^{(n)} := P \vee T^{-1}P \vee \dots \vee T^{-(n- 1)}P
      </math>where <math display="inline">P \vee Q</math> is the least upper bound partition, that is, the least refined partition that refines both <math display="inline">P</math> and <math display="inline">Q</math>:<math display="block">P\vee Q := \{p \cap q: p \in P, q \in Q\}</math>Write <math display="inline">P(x)</math> to be the set in <math display="inline">P</math> where <math display="inline">x</math> falls in. So, for example, <math display="inline">P^{(n)}(x)</math> is the <math display="inline">n</math>-letter initial segment of the <math display="inline">(P, T)</math> name of <math display="inline">x</math>.

Write <math display="inline">I_{P}(x)</math> to be the information (in units of ''[[nat (unit)|nats]]'') about <math display="inline">x</math> we can recover, if we know which element in the partition <math display="inline">P</math> that <math display="inline">x</math> falls in:<math display="block">I_{P} := -\ln \mu(P(x))</math>Similarly, the conditional information of partition <math display="inline">P</math>, conditional on partition <math display="inline">Q</math>, about <math display="inline">x</math>, is<math display="block">I_{P|Q}(x) := -\ln \frac{P\vee Q(x)}{Q(x)}</math><math display="inline">h_T(P)</math> is the [[Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy]]<math display="block">
      h_T(P) := \lim_n \frac 1n H(P^{(n)}) = \lim_n E_{x\sim \mu}\left[\frac 1n I_{P^{(n)}}(x)\right]
      </math>In other words, by definition, there is a convergence in expectation. The SMB theorem states that when <math display="inline">T</math> is ergodic, there is convergence in L1.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Petersen |first=Karl E. |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/ergodic-theory/4F50E2830B2812125F24D4A2CE7318D0 |title=Ergodic Theory |date=1983 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-38997-6 |series=Cambridge Studies in Advanced Mathematics |location=Cambridge |chapter=6.2. The Shannon–McMillan–Breiman Theorem}}</ref>

{{Math theorem
| name = Theorem
| note = ergodic case
| math_statement = If <math display="inline">T</math> is ergodic, then <math display="block">
      x \mapsto  \frac 1n I_{P^{(n)}}(x)
      </math> converges in L1 to the constant function <math display="inline">x \mapsto h_T(P)</math>.

In other words, <math display="block">
      E_{x\sim \mu}\left[ \left|\lim_n \frac 1n I_{P^{(n)}}(x) - h_T(P)\right|\right] = 0
      </math> 

In particular, since L1 convergence implies almost sure convergence, <math display="block">h_T(P) = \lim_n \frac 1n I_{P^{(n)}}(x)</math> with probability 1.
}}

{{Math theorem
| name = Corollary
| note = entropy equipartition property
| math_statement = <math display="inline">\forall \epsilon > 0, \exists N, \forall n \geq N</math>, we can partition the partition <math display="inline">\vee_{k=0}^{n-1} T^{-k}P</math> into two parts, the “good” part <math display="inline">G</math> and the “bad” part <math display="inline">B</math>.

The bad part is small: <math display="block">\sum_{b \in B}\mu(b) < \epsilon</math> 

The good part is almost equipartitioned according to entropy: <math display="block">
      \forall g\in G, \quad -\frac 1n \ln \mu(g) \in h_T(P) \pm \epsilon
      </math>
}}

If <math display="inline">T</math> is not necessarily ergodic, then the underlying probability space would be split up into multiple subsets, each invariant under <math display="inline">T</math>. In this case, we still have L1 convergence to some function, but that function is no longer a [[constant function]].<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Pollicott |first1=Mark |author1-link=Mark Pollicott |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/dynamical-systems-and-ergodic-theory/3C1AA7BE85F5D2EE027D60CC72FDBEB8 |title=Dynamical Systems and Ergodic Theory |last2=Yuri |first2=Michiko |date=1998 |publisher=Cambridge University Press |isbn=978-0-521-57294-1 |series=London Mathematical Society Student Texts |location=Cambridge |chapter=12.4. The Shannon–McMillan–Brieman theorem}}</ref>

{{Math theorem|name=Theorem|note=general case|math_statement=

Let <math display="inline">\mathcal I</math> be the sigma-algebra generated by all <math display="inline">T</math> -invariant measurable subsets of <math display="inline">\Omega</math>, - <math display="block">
      x \mapsto  \frac 1n I_{P^{(n)}}(x)
      </math> converges in L1 to<br />
<math display="block">
      x \mapsto E\left[\lim_n I_{P | \vee_{k = 1}^n T^{-k}P} \big|\; \mathcal I \right]
      </math>
}}

When <math display="inline">T</math> is ergodic, <math display="inline">\mathcal I</math> is trivial, and so the function<math display="block">
 x \mapsto E\left[ \lim_n I_{P | \vee_{k = 1}^n T^{-k}P} \big|\; \mathcal I \right]
 </math>simplifies into the constant function <math display="inline">x\mapsto E\left[ \lim_n I_{P | \vee_{k = 1}^n T^{-k}P} \right]</math>, which by definition, equals <math display="inline">\lim_n H(P | \vee_{k = 1}^n T^{-k}P)</math>, which equals <math display="inline">h_T(P)</math> by a proposition.

== Continuous-time stationary ergodic sources ==
Discrete-time functions can be interpolated to continuous-time functions. If such interpolation ''f'' is [[measurable]], we may define the continuous-time stationary process accordingly as <math>\tilde{X}:=f\circ X</math>. If the asymptotic equipartition property holds for the discrete-time process, as in the i.i.d. or finite-valued stationary ergodic cases shown above, it automatically holds for the continuous-time stationary process derived from it by some measurable interpolation. i.e.
<math display="block">-\frac{1}{n} \log p(\tilde{X}_0^\tau) \to H(X)</math>
where ''n'' corresponds to the degree of freedom in time {{math|''τ''}}. {{math|''nH''(''X'')/''τ''}} and {{math|''H''(''X'')}} are the entropy per unit time and per degree of freedom respectively, defined by [[Claude E. Shannon|Shannon]].

An important class of such continuous-time stationary process is the bandlimited stationary ergodic process with the [[sample space]] being a subset of the continuous <math>\mathcal{L}_2</math> functions. The asymptotic equipartition property holds if the process is white, in which case the time samples are i.i.d., or there exists ''T'' > 1/2''W'', where ''W'' is the [[Bandwidth (signal processing)|nominal bandwidth]], such that the ''T''-spaced time samples take values in a [[finite set]], in which case we have the discrete-time finite-valued stationary ergodic process.

Any [[time-invariant]] operations also preserves the asymptotic equipartition property, stationarity and ergodicity and we may easily turn a stationary process to non-stationary without losing the asymptotic equipartition property by nulling out a finite number of time samples in the process.

==Category theory==
A [[category theoretic]] definition for the equipartition property is given by [[Mikhael Gromov (mathematician)|Gromov]].<ref>[[Misha Gromov]] (2013). "[https://www.ihes.fr/~gromov/wp-content/uploads/2018/08/structre-serch-entropy-july5-2012.pdf In a Search for a Structure, Part 1: On Entropy]". ''(See page 5, where the equipartition property is called the 'Bernoulli approximation theorem'.)''</ref> Given a sequence of [[Product (category theory)|Cartesian powers]] <math>P^N=P\times \cdots \times P</math> of a measure space ''P'', this sequence admits an ''asymptotically equivalent'' sequence ''H<sub>N</sub>'' of homogeneous measure spaces (''i.e.'' all sets have the same measure; all morphisms are invariant under the group of automorphisms, and thus factor as a morphism to the [[terminal object]]).

The above requires a definition of ''asymptotic equivalence''. This is given in terms of a distance function, giving how much an [[injective correspondence]] differs from an [[isomorphism]].  An injective correspondence <math>\pi: P\to Q</math> is a [[partially defined map]] that is a [[bijection]]; that is, it is a bijection between a subset <math>P'\subset P</math> and <math>Q'\subset Q</math>.  Then define
<math display="block">|P-Q|_\pi = |P \setminus P'| + |Q \setminus Q'|,</math>
where |''S''| denotes the measure of a set ''S''.  In what follows, the measure of ''P'' and ''Q'' are taken to be 1, so that the measure spaces are probability spaces. This distance <math>|P-Q|_\pi</math> is commonly known as the [[earth mover's distance]] or [[Wasserstein metric]].

Similarly, define
<math display="block">|\log P:Q|_\pi = \frac{\sup_{p\in P'}|\log p - \log \pi(p)|}{\log \min \left(|\operatorname{set}(P')|,|\operatorname{set}(Q')|\right)}.</math>
with <math>|\operatorname{set}(P)|</math> taken to be the [[counting measure]] on ''P''.  Thus, this definition requires that ''P'' be a finite measure space.  Finally, let
<math display="block">\text{dist}_\pi(P,Q) = |P-Q|_\pi +|\log P:Q|_\pi.</math>

A sequence of injective correspondences <math>\pi_N:P_N\to Q_N</math> are then '''asymptotically equivalent''' when
<math display="block">\text{dist}_{\pi_N}(P_N,Q_N) \to 0 \quad\text{ as }\quad N\to\infty.</math>

Given a homogenous space sequence ''H<sub>N</sub>'' that is asymptotically equivalent to ''P<sup>N</sup>'', the entropy ''H''(''P'') of ''P'' may be taken as
<math display="block">H(P) = \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac{1}{N} |\operatorname{set}(H_N)|.</math>
